payload.claim: The holder writes its pid and text (lines 106-109) only after fcntl.flock already granted it the lock (line 102), not atomically with it. A contender that hits BlockingIOError in that narrow window reads whatever was in the file beforehand (empty on a lock file's first-ever use, or a previous, now-unrelated holder's stale line left over from an earlier release, since release never clears the file) rather than the current holder's real pid and text. The resulting LockHeld names a pid (possibly -1, possibly a dead, unrelated process) that is not actually holding anything, which would mislead whoever reads the refusal reason into chasing the wrong process. No test exercises this ordering because every witness's holder is already blocked on stdin well before the contender attempts the lock, so the gates cannot see it.
